932.title: The Maharaja close
932.hook: forty years of a Punjab kingdom, from Lahore's open gate to the samadhi
932.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharaja Ranjit Singh's reign as the time of a Sikh kingdom in the Punjab, and tell its story from his taking of Lahore to his death, and the troubles that followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach, and your line was pride and honesty. When you spoke about something you love, did you name what it got wrong? Today, we close the story of the Maharaja. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

Lay two pictures side by side. In the first, a young chief with one eye rides through a gate of Lahore that someone inside has opened for him. In the second, a pale building with a gilded dome stands by the same city's Fort, holding his ashes. Everything in this part of the path happened between those two pictures. Histories count about forty years from the day he took Lahore to the day he died. Today: the Maharaja close.
screen: `A GATE OPENED IN LAHORE.` → `A SAMADHI BY THE FORT.` → `EVERYTHING IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the rise. A boy born in Gujranwala, scarred by smallpox and blind in one eye, led his misl young, with help around him. Lahore opened its gate to him. He took the title of Maharaja, but ruled as the Sarkar-e-Khalsa, the government in the Khalsa's name. Second, what he built. Gold on the Harmandir. A river line on the Sutlej that he chose to keep. An army drilled in new ways by officers from many lands. Hari Singh Nalwa on the frontier. Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar joining the kingdom. The Koh-i-Noor on his arm. A court of many faiths, painters at work, gifts to Patna and Nanded, and a reputation for rarely ordering death. And Maharani Jind Kaur, the youngest queen, whose hardest days are still ahead. Third, what he couldn't hold. He bowed at the Akal Takht and accepted its rebuke, so even he answered to something above the throne. But he left no settled way to hand on what he'd built. After he died, the kingdom he'd held together came apart in the hands of rivals: two heirs lost, Sher Singh killed, a child on the throne, the army speaking louder than the court. A kingdom that was so much one man's work was fragile without him. Fourth, the shape of it. Forty years is a single working life. Long enough to build something that changed the map. Short enough that people who saw it begin could see it end. That's the sorrow in this story, and the honesty too. Some things are great and brief at once. Tomorrow, a new part of the path begins, and it's harder: war with the British.

segments.voice: Two minutes with something that ended too soon. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind something in your life that was good and didn't last as long as you wanted: a friendship, a home, a job, a season, a person. Picture its beginning first. Then what it built in you. Then the end. Don't rush past the end. Let it be what it was. Then notice what's still with you from it, even now. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sher-e-Punjab, the Lion of the Punjab, the name Sikhs give Ranjit Singh, whose story ends here, from Lahore's open gate to his samadhi, and a kingdom that came apart without him. Today's word.
Your line: forty years. Today, thank someone for something good that ended, even if it ended too soon. Day nine hundred thirty-two.

933.title: War with the British, 1845
933.hook: the Khalsa army crosses the Sutlej, and battles are fought at Mudki and Ferozeshah
933.howItsDone: Sikhs remember the opening battles of the war with the British, including Mudki and Ferozeshah, as a time of great courage by the Khalsa soldiers and of failure by some of their commanders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sher-e-Punjab, and your line was forty years. Who did you thank for something good that ended? Today a new part of the path begins: loss and exile. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

The Sutlej again. This is the river Ranjit Singh chose as a border with the British, and kept. On one bank, the Punjab. On the other, British India, where new regiments and guns have been arriving at the river towns. Now, on a winter's day, the Khalsa army is crossing that river with its guns and horses. The line the old Maharaja held for so long is being stepped over. Today: war with the British.
screen: `THE SUTLEJ, THE OLD BORDER.` → `BRITISH TROOPS AT THE RIVER TOWNS.` → `THE KHALSA ARMY CROSSES.`

segments.voice: First, how it came. Histories tell it from more than one side. The British had been gathering troops near the Sutlej, and in Lahore that looked like a threat. The Khalsa army, proud and restless, was ready to fight. And Cunningham, the British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, suggests that some leaders at the court were glad to send the army against the British, hoping it would be broken. So war came from fear, pride and plotting all at once. Second, Mudki. The opening battle was fought near a village called Mudki, late in the day, in dust and failing light. The British held the field. Third, Ferozeshah. Days later came a fiercer fight around the Sikh camp at Ferozeshah. The Khalsa soldiers fought hard behind their guns, and British accounts admit how close their own army came to disaster. But the Sikh army's commanders, Lal Singh and Tej Singh, made choices in those days that Sikh memory still questions, and the chance was lost. You'll hear more of that tomorrow. Fourth, how to stand in a conflict. In a verse of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Ninth Guru, the wise one is described as frightening no one and afraid of no one. That's not a battle plan. It's a way to stand inside a storm without losing your center: not ruled by fear, and not ruling others by it. The soldiers at Ferozeshah showed the fearless half. Some at the court that sent them, as Cunningham tells it, were ruled by fear of their own army. That's today's line.

Your line: war came. Today, when a conflict rises, take one slow breath before you answer, and answer from your feet, not your temper. Day nine hundred thirty-three.

934.title: Sobraon, 1846
934.hook: the Sikh army is defeated on the Sutlej, and Sikh memory holds that some of its own commanders betrayed it
934.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Sobraon with grief and honor, telling of Sham Singh Attariwala and the soldiers trapped at the river, and of commanders Sikh memory holds to have betrayed them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nirbhau, and your line was war came. When a conflict rose, did you take that breath first? Today, the battle that ended that war. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

An old general gets dressed for battle in white. Sikh tradition remembers him that way: Sham Singh Attariwala, gray-bearded, in white clothes, mounting his horse on the morning of the fight. In that telling, the white means he didn't expect to come home. Behind him the Sikh army is dug in along the bank of the Sutlej, with a bridge of boats at its back. In front of it, the British are forming up. Today: Sobraon.
screen: `AN OLD GENERAL IN WHITE.` → `DUG IN ON THE SUTLEJ.` → `A BRIDGE OF BOATS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: First, the battle. At Sobraon the Khalsa army held strong earthworks on the river, and the British attacked them head on. The fighting was fierce, and for a time the Sikh lines held. Then the British broke through, and the Sikh soldiers were pushed back toward the river. Second, the bridge. Behind them stood the bridge of boats, their road home. Accounts say that Tej Singh, the commander, crossed back over it early, and that the bridge then broke, whether by the river, by the weight of men, or, as some tell it, by someone's order. With the bridge gone, soldiers were trapped against the water. Many died in the Sutlej that day, histories say, and few surrendered. Third, Sham Singh. The old general in white rode into the fighting and fell there. Sikh memory holds him up beside the trapped soldiers as the honor of that day: men who were let down, and fought on anyway. Fourth, the betrayal. Sikh memory holds that the army's own commanders, Tej Singh and the minister Lal Singh, betrayed it, sending word to the British and leading their own soldiers badly on purpose. Cunningham, the British officer who wrote a history of the Sikhs, said much the same. Some historians weigh the evidence differently. But the hurt in the story isn't hard to understand. An enemy across the river is expected. A commander behind you who wants you to lose is something else. That's today's line.

Just let your breath go there, and let it be held. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sobraon. The battle on the Sutlej where the Khalsa army was defeated, the bridge of boats gave way, and Sham Singh Attariwala fell. Today's word.
Your line: betrayal hurts most. Today, keep one small promise to someone who's counting on you, exactly as you made it. Day nine hundred thirty-four.

935.title: The treaty and Kashmir
935.hook: Punjab loses land, and Kashmir is sold to Gulab Singh
935.howItsDone: Sikh histories remember the treaties after the war with the British as a loss made on paper, in which the Punjab gave up land and Kashmir passed to Gulab Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sobraon, and your line was betrayal hurts most. Did you keep that small promise exactly as you made it? Today the fighting is over, and the talking starts. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

No guns this time. A table, papers, ink, men in good coats. On one side, British officials. On the other, ministers speaking for a boy Maharaja who isn't old enough to read what's being signed. The British army is camped at Lahore. Everyone at that table knows who won at Sobraon. What's left is to write down what it will cost. Land the Khalsa held is about to change hands without a shot. Today: the treaty and Kashmir.
screen: `A TABLE, PAPERS AND INK.` → `A BOY MAHARAJA'S MINISTERS.` → `WRITING DOWN THE COST.`

segments.voice: First, the land. Under the treaty of Lahore, the kingdom gave up the fertile country between the Beas and the Sutlej rivers. The old river line that Ranjit Singh had kept was pushed back into the heart of the Punjab. The Khalsa army was cut down in size, and British troops stayed in Lahore. Second, the money. The British also demanded a large payment for the cost of the war. The treasury in Lahore couldn't meet it. So in place of the money, the British took Kashmir and the hill country around it. Third, the sale. Then, in a second treaty at Amritsar, the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh, the Dogra raja of Jammu. You met him at the court of many faiths, one of the Dogra brothers who served the Maharaja. In the war he had kept out of the fighting and acted as a go-between with the British. Now he became the ruler of the valley the Sikh army had once climbed the passes to win. Kashmiris themselves were not asked. Fourth, the feeling. Sobraon was a battlefield, and Sikh memory honors the men who fell there. The treaty is remembered differently: as a loss made quietly, by signatures, with a raja who had served the court walking away as ruler of Kashmir. Some losses don't happen in the fight. They happen afterward, on paper, while the people affected aren't in the room. That's today's line.
screen: `THE LAND BETWEEN TWO RIVERS.` · `A PAYMENT THAT COULDN'T BE MET.` · `KASHMIR SOLD TO GULAB SINGH.` · `A LOSS MADE ON PAPER.` · then, large: `LOST AT A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a loss you didn't choose. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind something you lost because of a decision made somewhere else: a job cut in a meeting you weren't in, a move you didn't pick, a plan someone else canceled. Notice it without arguing with it. Let your breath be slow and even. Then notice one thing that's still yours, that no table could sign away. Rest there. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Sandhi, a treaty, a peace made with ink rather than swords: land given up after the war, and the valley taken in place of money and sold to Gulab Singh. Today's word.
Your line: lost at a table. Today, when a decision is made about someone who isn't in the room, ask what they would say, or make sure they hear it. Day nine hundred thirty-five.

936.title: The queen exiled
936.hook: Maharani Jind Kaur is separated from her son and sent away
936.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Maharani Jind Kaur, often called Rani Jindan, as a queen and mother who resisted British control and was separated from her son, Maharaja Duleep Singh.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sandhi, and your line was lost at a table. Whose voice did you bring into a room they weren't in? Today, the treaties reach the palace, and a mother. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

A carriage waits in a palace courtyard in Lahore. The woman being taken to it has ruled the Punjab in her son's name. She has argued with ministers, faced down the army's councils, and spoken her mind to British officials. Now there are guards at her side, and the boy Maharaja is not coming with her. Somewhere in the palace behind her is her son. She is being sent away from him. Today: the queen exiled.
screen: `A CARRIAGE IN THE COURTYARD.` → `GUARDS AT HER SIDE.` → `HER SON STAYS BEHIND.`

segments.voice: First, the power taken. After the war, a new agreement put the Punjab's government in the hands of a council of the court's chiefs and ministers, guided by a British Resident at Lahore. Maharani Jind Kaur, who had been regent, was set aside with a pension. Her son stayed on the throne. She no longer had any say in how he was raised or how his kingdom was run. Second, the charge. The British Resident came to believe she was plotting against the new order, and histories record accusations of a plot against British officials. She denied it, and the evidence is still argued over. Whatever the truth, the decision was made. She was taken from Lahore to the fort at Sheikhupura, some miles from the city, and the boy was kept at the palace. Later she was sent much further, out of the Punjab altogether. Third, the mother. Histories record her protests, sharp and grieving, against being parted from her child. She asked for her son. She wasn't given him. The boy, too young to choose anything, stayed among officials and tutors. Fourth, how she is remembered. Sikh memory calls her Rani Jindan and holds her up as a mother and a queen who would not bow quietly, even when she lost. Some British writers of the time painted her as dangerous; Sikh tellings remember her courage. Both views appear in the histories, and today's story belongs to her grief. A crown can be taken by treaty. Taking a child from his mother is a different kind of loss. That's today's line.
screen: `SET ASIDE WITH A PENSION.` · `A CHARGE OF PLOTTING.` · `SHE ASKED FOR HER SON.` · `RANI JINDAN, WHO WOULD NOT BOW.` · then, large: `MOTHER AND SON APART.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a mother apart from her child. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind any mother who is far from her child today: across a border, in a hospital, in a prison, separated by work, by war, by a court's decision, or by death. You don't need to know her name. Maharani, great queen, the title by which Jind Kaur is remembered: set aside, accused, and sent away from Lahore, while her son, the boy Maharaja, stayed behind. Today's word.
Your line: mother and son apart. Today, call or write to a parent, or a child, or someone who is one to you, and just let them hear your voice. Day nine hundred thirty-six.

937.title: Multan rises, 1848
937.hook: a handover at a fortress city, an attack at the gate, and a revolt that leads to a second war
937.howItsDone: Sikh histories tell the rising at Multan as the start of the second war with the British, a local quarrel over a handover that grew into a war for the whole Punjab.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maharani, and your line was mother and son apart. Who came to mind, far from someone they love? Today, far from Lahore, a city catches fire. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

Multan, a walled fortress city in the south of the Punjab. Its governor, Diwan Mulraj, has said he will step down. A new governor rides in to take his place, and British officers from Lahore ride with him. They look over the fort. They receive the keys. Then they turn their horses toward the gate to ride back out, and a soldier of the garrison steps forward with a spear. Within days the city is in open revolt, and before long the Punjab is at war again. Today: Multan rises.
screen: `A FORTRESS CITY IN THE SOUTH.` → `THE KEYS ARE HANDED OVER.` → `A SPEAR AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: First, the handover. After the first war with the British, officers from the East India Company sat close to the court at Lahore and had a heavy hand in its decisions. Mulraj had governed Multan for the court, and he was in a dispute with Lahore over the revenue the province owed. He offered to resign, and a new governor was sent down with British officers to take charge. Second, the attack at the gate. As the officers left the fort, men of the garrison set on them and wounded them. They took shelter outside the walls, and soon after, they were killed there. Third, the question that has never been fully settled. Did Mulraj give the order? Some histories say he planned the rising from the start. Others say his own soldiers struck first and he was swept along, unable or unwilling to turn back once blood had been shed. Herbert Edwardes, a British officer who gathered local fighters and marched on Multan, wrote his own account, and even his story leaves room for doubt. Fourth, how a spark became a war. The revolt spread. Other Sikh leaders, angry at a kingdom now run from outside, joined it, among them Sher Singh Attariwala. And the governor-general, Lord Dalhousie, chose not a local settlement but a second war. In the saloks of Sheikh Farid, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, Farid tells the reader to answer evil with good and not to let anger fill the mind. A spear at a gate is a small thing. At Multan, it set a whole country burning. That's today's line.
screen: `A GOVERNOR STEPS DOWN.` · `AN ATTACK AT THE GATE.` · `WHO GAVE THE ORDER?` · `A SPARK BECOMES A WAR.` · then, large: `THE SPARK.`

If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Multan rises. A handover at a fortress city turns into an attack at the gate, and the attack becomes the revolt that leads to a second war. Today's word.

938.title: Chillianwala, 1849
938.hook: a battle in thick scrub near the Jhelum, fought into the dark, and a Sikh army that would not give way
938.howItsDone: Sikh histories and tellings remember Chillianwala as a battle where the Khalsa army stood its ground against the British, and the story is told with pride alongside the losses that followed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Multan rises, and your line was the spark. Did you catch one small spark before it caught? Today, the fire that spark started reaches a field by a river. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.

Late afternoon, near the river Jhelum. The ground ahead is thick with thorny scrub, so dense a soldier can barely see the man beside him. Somewhere in it waits the Sikh army under Sher Singh Attariwala. The British commander, Lord Gough, had meant to wait for morning. Instead, with the light already going, he orders the attack. Regiments push forward into the thorns, and the guns open up from places nobody can see. Today: Chillianwala.
screen: `THORNY SCRUB BY THE JHELUM.` → `THE LIGHT IS GOING.` → `GOUGH ORDERS THE ATTACK.`

segments.voice: First, the ground. The Sikh army had chosen its position well, behind cover, with its guns ready. The scrub broke up the British lines. Units lost touch with each other. Some charged straight into fire they couldn't see until it hit them. Second, the fighting. It was close and it was bloody. Accounts from the British side describe regiments cut up, guns lost, and men falling back in confusion. On the Sikh side, an army that had lost at Sobraon, and seen land lost at the treaty table, fought hard and gave little away. Third, the dark. Night came down on a field where nobody had clearly won. The British held part of the ground, and claimed the day. The Sikh army drew back in good order, still an army, still ready to fight. When the news reached Britain, it was received as a shock, and a new commander was sent out to replace Gough. Fourth, what the Sikhs keep. In the Guru Granth Sahib, a salok of Bhagat Kabir says the true hero is the one who fights for the helpless (some read it, for the faith), and who, even cut to pieces, never leaves the field. In Sikh tellings, Chillianwala is held up as that kind of day: no throne won, nothing changed on the map, but an army that stood its ground. And a look back at the week. It began with a kingdom's close and the first war, then Sobraon and the treaty, the queen sent away, and the spark at Multan. Each day, something taken. Today, something kept. That's today's line.
screen: `A STRONG POSITION IN THE SCRUB.` · `CLOSE, BLOODY FIGHTING.` · `NIGHT, AND NO CLEAR WINNER.` · `THE HERO NEVER LEAVES THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THEY HELD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes of holding still. Sit with both feet flat on the floor, and feel the ground under them. Let your breath settle low in your body. Now bring to mind one place where you usually give way when you'd rather not: a conversation where you go quiet, a habit that wins every evening, a pressure at work. You don't have to fight it now. Just feel your feet on the floor, and picture yourself, next time, staying where you are for one breath longer. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Chillianwala. A battle in thick scrub near the Jhelum, fought into the dark, with no clear winner and a Sikh army that held its ground. Today's word.
Your line: they held. Today, stand your ground once, kindly and plainly, in one small place where you usually give way. Day nine hundred thirty-eight.
